desc:
Given a rows × cols matrix of integers (which may be negative) and an integer k, consider every rectangular block of cells made of consecutive rows and consecutive columns. Return the largest block sum that is not greater than k.

It is guaranteed that at least one block has a sum of at most k, so an answer always exists. Checking every rectangle with prefix sums is O(rows² · cols²); aim for something closer to O(rows² · cols · log cols).

matrix = [[1, 0, 1], [0, -2, 3]], k = 2  →  2
(the block [[0, 1], [-2, 3]] sums to 2)

matrix = [[2, 2, -1]], k = 3  →  3
constraints: min(matrix) ≤ k ≤ 100,000, so at least one block has sum ≤ k
hints: Fix a pair of rows (top and bottom). Squash everything between them into one array of column sums. The problem becomes one-dimensional.
In 1D: the best subarray ending at position j with sum ≤ k needs a previous prefix sum p with cur - p ≤ k, and you want the smallest such p (so that cur - p is as large as possible).

Keep the earlier prefix sums in a sorted list. For the current prefix cur binary-search the first element ≥ cur - k, update the best answer with cur - that, then insert cur into the list. Loop over row pairs on the smaller dimension to keep the cost down.
editorial: Choose the top row and the bottom row of the rectangle, and let col[j] be the sum of column j between them; adding a new bottom row just adds that row to col. A rectangle with those rows corresponds to a subarray of col, so the task becomes: find the maximum subarray sum not exceeding k in a 1D array.

For the 1D part, keep a sorted list of prefix sums seen so far (starting with 0). When the running prefix sum is cur, a subarray ending here has sum cur - p for each earlier prefix p, and we need cur - p ≤ k, i.e. p ≥ cur - k. The best choice is the smallest p satisfying that, found by binary search (bisect_left). Then insert cur into the sorted list.

The total is O(R² · C log C) comparisons, plus the cost of list insertions. Choose the dimension that is smaller for the pair-of-lines loop (transpose when rows > cols) to minimise the multiplied factor. If any 1D result equals k exactly, you can stop at once because nothing can beat k.
